title: What else can be compared by laying one on another?
description: Two line segments are compared with one end of each together, two squares with a corner on a corner, and two circles with the centre on the centre. In each case the shape that sticks out is the larger one. Keeko's doubt is that laying one over another works only for angles.
teaching_notes: One idea: superimposition compares any two shapes of the same kind, by matching one common part and seeing which one sticks out. Watch for students who think the method belongs only to angles.

source: Where else do we use superimposition to compare?
video_script.why: The child sees that superimposition compares line segments, squares and circles as well as angles.
video_script.substitution: the book's question on where else superimposition is used, with line segments, squares and circles
video_script.anchor: pairs of line segments, squares and circles laid one over another
video_script.wrong_answer: placing one over another works only for angles
video_script.wrong_move: thinks superimposition belongs only to angles
video_script.payoff_line: We can compare line segments, squares and circles by laying one over another
maths_rules: line segments: put one end of each together along the same line and see where the other ends fall
squares: put a corner on a corner with the sides along each other and see whether the other sides overlap
circles: put the centre on the centre and see whether the edges overlap or one lies outside the other
if everything overlaps exactly, the two shapes are equal in size
if one sticks out, that one is larger
slip: the method is not only for angles
video_script.design: One idea: lay one shape over another, matching one common part, and see which sticks out. Three pairs of shapes stay on the board. Keeko's doubt: only angles can be laid over one another.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; two angles, one traced and laid over the other

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.angles: the traced angle lies over the other angle
marks.ask: a question mark rises beside the angles

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='angles'/>We compared two angles by laying a copy of one over the other.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Where else can we compare in this way?

beats.on_screen: the two angles stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one shape sliding over another shape of the same kind
narration: <bookmark mark='slide'/>Placing one shape over another to compare them is called superimposition.
<bookmark mark='name'/>We match one part of the two shapes first, and then we look at the rest.

marks.given: the words are written beside the two angles

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, superimposition compares two angles by laying one over the other.

beats.on_screen: To find: other things we can compare in this way

marks.find: the words other things are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find other things that can be compared in this way.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: two line segments, one end of each together on the same line

marks.ends: two line segments are laid with one end of each together
marks.far: the longer segment sticks out past the other

narration: <bookmark mark='ends'/>Step one, take two line segments. Put one end of each together, along the same line.
<bookmark mark='far'/>The segment whose other end reaches farther is the longer one.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: two squares, a corner on a corner, sides along each other

marks.corner: two squares are laid with a corner on a corner
marks.stick: the larger square sticks out past the smaller one

narration: <bookmark mark='corner'/>Step two, take two squares. Put a corner on a corner, with the sides along each other.
<bookmark mark='stick'/>If the other sides overlap, the squares are equal. If one sticks out, that one is larger.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: two circles, centre on centre

marks.centre: two circles are laid with centre on centre
marks.edge: the edge of the larger circle lies outside the other

narration: <bookmark mark='centre'/>Step three, take two circles. Put the centre on the centre.
<bookmark mark='edge'/>If the edges overlap, the circles are equal. If one edge lies outside, that circle is larger.

beats.on_screen: Answer: line segments, squares and circles
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>We can compare line segments, squares and circles by laying one over another.
There are many more shapes that can be compared in this way.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: two squares laid corner on corner, the larger one sticking out; the angle-only claim is struck through

marks.doubt: the claim appears on the board
marks.tile: two squares are laid corner on corner

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks placing one over another works only for angles.
<bookmark mark='tile'/>But lay one square on another with the corners together, and the larger square sticks out.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Squares are not angles, and the idea works for them too.
